signals.source_text: Five years ago I was implementing an LQR attitude controller for a VTOL aircraft inside a PX4 SITL environment. Today I validate control performance on real vehicles. During my graduate research I worked in two PX4-Autopilot software-in-the-loop setups, each for a different reason. In PX4 with Gazebo I implemented an LQR attitude controller for quadrotor and VTOL airframes in vertical take-off and landing mode, validated it in SITL, then put it on a scaled unmanned aircraft and flew it. In PX4 with JSBSim I built the environment around a high-fidelity aerodynamic model of the VTOL aircraft, because there the fidelity of the aerodynamics was what mattered. Alongside that I derived a tilt schedule for transition flight from trim analysis. Flying a controller you tuned in simulation is where the real question shows up: what survives the trip from simulation to hardware, and what quietly does not. Later work on a Digital Twin collaboration sharpened it into a name — the Sim-to-Real gap. Since then the applications have kept changing. Published reinforcement-learning-based transition-flight research on the aerospace side. Real-vehicle control performance development and validation on the automotive side. Different vehicles, different teams, same underlying problem: connecting models, control logic, learning-based methods, and validation so that an autonomous physical system behaves reliably outside the simulator. That intersection — learning, control, simulation, autonomy — is also where I want to keep going. I am starting this series to write the thread down, one piece at a time. First up: the PX4 scaled-UAV loop, from SITL to flight test. --- 학생 시절 두 가지 PX4 SITL 환경을 다뤘습니다. PX4-Gazebo에서는 Quadrotor와 VTOL 기체의 수직이착륙 모드 LQR 자세제어기를 구현해 SITL에서 검증한 뒤, 축소기에 탑재해 비행 시험까지 수행했습니다. PX4-JSBSim은 VTOL 기체의 공력 모델을 고충실도로 쓰기 위한 환경으로 구축했습니다. 이와 함께 trim 해석 기반 천이 비행 tilt schedule을 도출했습니다. 이후 Digital Twin 협업, 강화학습 기반 천이 비행 연구, 실차 제어 성능 검증을 거치며 시뮬레이션과 실제 물리 시스템을 연결하는 문제에 계속 붙어 있었습니다. 학습·제어·시뮬레이션·자율성이 만나는 지점으로 계속 나아가려 합니다. 그 기록을 하나씩 정리해 보려 합니다. #SimToReal #AutonomousSystems #ControlSystems #VehicleDynamics #eVTOL

signals.source_text: I was on the road to Fort Worth at 5:30 in the morning for the launch of Project Nexus, Texas's eIPP program. It brings industry, lawmakers, and agencies together to help enable and scale safe commercial operations of electrically powered, autonomy-enabled aircraft. That meant a visit to the increasingly familiar Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport , watching Christopher Ash, C.M., ACE and team welcome a genuine all-star cast from government and the advanced air mobility industry to the stage. Beyond the conversations, the real privilege is getting up close with these aircraft. Not many people outside these companies and the government get to see them fly. That meant standing under the wing of Joby Aviation ’s autonomy-enabled Caravan, picking out the Ouster LiDAR unit and the Echodyne radar, the Team USA livery on Archer ’s Midnight, and the Texas flag on the tail of Joby's S4. Merlin ’s shark-teeth nose art was unsubtle and kickass, with a Silvus radio mounted inside the plane. This isn't meant to be a commercial for AUVSI — Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International members, but it's a good sign so many of the companies flying are part of our growing membership. Much like my own decade in this industry, plenty of these companies have been working toward this exact moment just as long, if not longer. It was energizing to hear Secretary Duffy push other states to be more like Texas and take U.S. Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration up on the authority they're willing to hand off. Half-joking, he told every Texan in the room to find Senator Cruz and let him know Duffy needs another $30 billion to finish his plan for BNATCS. Cruz pointed back to the 2024 FAA reauthorization and his own work writing the requirements for the Center for Advanced Aviation Technology. This wasn't my first time watching an eVTOL fly. That was 2023, at the Joby Field Trip in California, standing next to former acting FAA Administrator Dan Elwell, both of us in awe. What was new today was multiple aircraft operating at an airport that's anything but sleepy, Amazon Prime Air cargo runs and Air Force aircraft in the mix alongside everything else. With a jet APU humming and that kind of heavy traffic in the pattern, the backdrop made a better case for eVTOL than any quiet test flight could. It just sounded like part of the airport. This was its own kind of full-circle moment, watching the S4 fly alongside the nimble flight of BETA TECHNOLOGIES and Merlin's pilot-enabled autonomous plane, the first time I'd seen either of those two in the air. Thank you to Dan Harmon and Sergio Roman II for continuing to bring AUVSI into this ongoing work in Texas. Proud to call this state home, and looking forward to this integration and growth continuing until it becomes boring.

signals.source_text: Can a vertiport actually make money? I started from the bottom up — not with projected passenger demand, but with the smallest functional facility I could model: 1 TLOF, 2 stands, charging, ARFF and a 1,000 sqm terminal. The result surprised me. At full capacity, the facility generates about ₹3.4 crore in annual revenue, yet the project IRR is only around 2% — before land and taxes. The problem is not simply CAPEX. It is how much revenue a vertiport can extract from each four-seat aircraft movement without damaging the operator's economics. This is Part 1. The next question is whether a network of vertiports changes the economics. #Vertiports #AdvancedAirMobility #AirportPlanning #Aviation #InfrastructureFinance https://lnkd.in/dh8sNJnF
